title: Contributing
text: Bug fixes, tests and ports are welcome. A change should come with a test that fails without it. Before you send a change make check analyze verif-sim format-check make check : unit, CLI and integration tests ( SKIP_INTEGRATION=1 for the unit tests only). make analyze : gcc -fanalyzer , which must be silent, and clang-tidy. make verif-sim : the model-checking harnesses as random tests. make format-check : .clang-format (4 spaces, attached braces, char *p , 120 columns). make format rewrites files. CI pins clang-format 18, because the output differs between major versions. If you changed the controller, the process table or an iterator, also run sh tools/mutation.sh ; every mutant must still be killed, and a new defect class deserves a new mutant in tools/mutants.txt . Rules of the code base Architecture first. The module rules and invariants in ARCHITECTURE.md are normative: a change that breaks one changes that document in the same commit. Only src/main.c calls exit() ; only src/platform/*/iterator.c knows an operating system. Compatibility. Options, exit statuses and log text are the public interface of 1.x. A change a script could notice is listed in Upgrading and the changelog. Say what is not tested. Code that was written without a host to run it on is labelled that way in the source, the changelog and Platforms . A claim in the docs is a statement about a run that happened. Original code. Contributions are GPL-2.0-or-later. New files carry the copyright and SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later header used in the tree; contributors are credited in AUTHORS . Adding a platform Create src/platform/<os>/iterator.c with init_process_iterator , get_next_process and close_process_iterator , and add its branch to src/platform/iterator.c and the fields it needs to struct process_iterator in iterator.h . Fill struct process : pid, parent pid, a start time that is stable for the life of a process and only ever compared for equality, and CPU time in milliseconds. Document the units in iterator.h . Copy the processes into an array whose records start with struct snap_rec and call snapshot_select(recs, n, sizeof(*recs), filter->pid, filter->include_children) . Skip zombies and kernel threads. Check what your kernel really reports for them: OpenBSD listed zombies, and a limiter that waits for them never finishes. Check how the CPU clock advances. A counter that only moves when a process is switched out (OpenBSD's p_rtime ) makes the controller see steps, not a rate. Add a job to .github/workflows/vm.yml if a VM exists for it ( tools/vm_build.sh builds and tests inside the guest and keeps the transcript), and update Platforms with what actually ran. Sending a change Open a pull request at GitHub , or send a patch from git format-patch . Keep commits focused, explain the reason and the evidence (which test fails before and passes after) in the message, and do not mix a reformat with a behaviour change.

title: FAQ and troubleshooting
text: A process stays stopped after cpulimit died If cpulimit is killed with SIGKILL , or by the out-of-memory killer, or crashes while the target is in its stop slice, the target stays stopped (state T in ps ). No user-space program can prevent this; a supervising process could, but it would bring back the original's orphaned-limiter defect. Resume the target: kill -CONT 1234 pkill -CONT -f 'the command line' # or by name A normal stop of cpulimit ( SIGINT , SIGTERM , SIGHUP , SIGQUIT , the target exiting, an error) always sends SIGCONT first. Use those, not SIGKILL , to stop a limiter. The limit seems to have no effect Another user's process. If cpulimit may not signal it, it says Process found but you aren't allowed to control it and does nothing. Run it as that user or as root. The percentage is of one CPU. -l 50 on a program using four threads still allows half a CPU in total; -l 200 allows two. The children are not included. A shell script's work happens in its children: add -i . -m is too high. Processes using less than M of a CPU are never stopped. Remember -m 0.05 is 5 %, not -m 5 . Wrong pid. -p exits when the pid ends (it implies -z ); -e waits for a match unless -z is given. "already limited" and exit status 1 Another cpulimit holds the lock for that process (see one limiter per target ). The message names its pid. Stop that one, or pass --no-lock if you really want two limiters; they will undo each other's stop and continue and the result is not a clean limit. How accurate is it? Within a few points of the requested share on a quiet machine, with the same bias as the original: it delivers slightly less than asked at 10 % to 25 % and overshoots by a point or two near 50 %. See the measurements . Shorter chunks ( -c ) track the limit more closely and cost more wake-ups. On a busy or emulated machine the CPU accounting itself is coarse (one clock tick, 10 ms at 100 Hz), and so is the limit. Does it limit threads separately? No. The target is limited as a whole: the signals go to the process, so all of its threads stop and continue together. A two-thread busy loop at -l 50 measured 53 to 54 % of one CPU over 10 s, with the old and the new binary alike. Does it work with nice, ionice, taskset, chrt, timeout? Yes, and the integration tests check each: a target started under nice , ionice , taskset or chrt is limited and keeps its nice value, I/O class, CPU affinity and scheduling policy; cpulimit -l N nice -n 5 cmd limits cmd (the wrapper replaces itself with the command, so cpulimit's child is the command) and returns its exit status. A wrapper that stays alive and forks, such as timeout or setsid -w , is the child cpulimit sees: add -i to reach the command below it. Running cpulimit itself under nice , ionice or taskset works too; a nice value you give it is kept with --no-boost and may be improved without it, if you have the privilege. Why not nice, cgroups or a scheduler class? nice only changes who wins when the CPU is contended; an idle machine still gives the process all of it. cgroup CPU quotas ( cpu.max , systemd-run -p CPUQuota= ) are the right tool on Linux when you control the service and have the privilege; they are enforced by the kernel and need no cpulimit process. cpulimit is for the cases where those are unavailable or too heavy: an already running process, another unix, a user without cgroup delegation, or a quick cap on one command. Containers cpulimit sees the processes of the PID namespace it runs in. To limit a container's process from the host, use the host pid; from inside, the container's. A cgroup CPU quota on the container applies in addition to the limit. Pid reuse A process is the pair (pid, start time); when a pid is recycled for a new process, cpulimit sees a new entry and does not limit it. A window of one control cycle remains between reading a process and signalling it, which no user-space program can close. Why does -h exit with 1? Every release of cpulimit has, and scripts may depend on it. -V exits 0. Where does a daemon log? To standard output and error as long as they exist, and with -s to syslog (facility LOG_DAEMON ). A daemon detaches from the terminal, so use -s to keep a record. Reporting a problem Open an issue at GitHub with the version ( cpulimit -V ), the system, the command line and, for a limit that does not hold, the output of the same command with -v .

title: How it works
text: cpulimit does not change priorities or scheduling classes. It lets the target run for part of a short chunk and stops it for the rest, and adjusts the split after every chunk from the CPU time the target really used. The control loop One iteration, repeated for as long as there is a target: Update the process table and compute each process's CPU usage since the last cycle. Compute the slices: compute_slices(limit, usage, previous rate, chunk) returns a work slice and a stop slice that add up to the chunk (default 100 ms). Send SIGCONT to everything, wait for the work slice, send SIGSTOP (skipping processes below the -m threshold), wait for the stop slice. Illustration of the idea, not measured data. The controller The controller is a pure function, compute_slices , with four invariants that are tested exhaustively on a grid and are the target of the bounded model checker: 0 ≤ work ≤ chunk and work + stop = chunk ; the rate is in [0, 1] and never NaN; no floating-point exception for any finite input; where the older formula was well defined, the result agrees with it to 1 ns. Accuracy is a property of this controller, shared with the original program: both under-deliver at low limits and overshoot near 50 % ( measurements ). Process identity A process is the pair (pid, start time). A new process that reuses a pid is a new entry, so a recycled pid is never limited by mistake (the original asserted and aborted). Each update stamps the entries it sees with a generation number and frees the rest, so the table is as large as the number of live processes and no larger. Every allocation is checked, and the unit tests fail the k-th allocation for every k to prove the table stays valid and leak-free. Signals and shutdown The handler for SIGINT , SIGTERM , SIGHUP and SIGQUIT only stores the signal number in a volatile sig_atomic_t . The four signals are blocked except inside the wait, which is a pselect() with the original mask, so a signal can neither be lost between checking the flag and sleeping nor delay shutdown by more than one wake-up. sleep() and nanosleep() alone cannot close that race. Invariant: never strand a target. Whenever the control loop is left for any reason (target ended, signal, allocation failure, error), every process cpulimit may have stopped receives SIGCONT before exit. The exception is outside the program's power: SIGKILL , an OOM kill or a crash during a stop slice leaves the target stopped ( what to do ). Timing uses CLOCK_MONOTONIC , so wall-clock steps cannot distort the duty cycle. Process iterators Everything that knows how an operating system lists processes lives in src/platform/<os>/iterator.c ; nothing else includes platform code, and a new platform is one file plus a branch in src/platform/iterator.c . The iterator answers one question: which processes does this filter select, and how much CPU has each used? System Source of the data CPU time Identity (start time) Linux /proc/<pid>/stat , parsed by a fuzzed, allocation-free parser utime + stime clock ticks ticks since boot macOS proc_listpids and proc_pidinfo mach time, converted with the timebase (not nanoseconds on Apple silicon) µs since the epoch FreeBSD kvm_getprocs (no group membership needed) ki_runtime , µs µs since the epoch OpenBSD sysctl kern.proc , no libkvm statistics tick counters ( p_uticks + p_sticks + p_iticks ) µs since the epoch NetBSD sysctl kern.proc2 , shares the OpenBSD code the same tick counters µs since the epoch Solaris, illumos /proc/<pid>/psinfo pr_time , ns seconds On OpenBSD the obvious field, p_rtime , is wrong for this purpose: the kernel only adds to it when a process is switched out, so a process that holds the CPU for a whole scheduling quantum appears to use nothing and then twice its share. The iterator reads the statistics tick counters instead, which the kernel advances on every statistics clock tick. Snapshots and the process tree The Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD and NetBSD iterators copy the processes into a snapshot when they start and then yield from it, so the answer is consistent even while processes come and go. The selection of "the target and all its descendants" ( -i ) is one shared function, snapshot_select() in src/platform/snapshot.c : it sorts an index by parent pid and walks it breadth first, O(n log n), visiting each record once, so a pid that is its own parent cannot loop. Zombies and kernel threads are never reported: they cannot use CPU. Further reading The normative description, including the module rules and the lock protocol, is docs/ARCHITECTURE.md in the repository; a change that breaks a rule there has to change that document in the same commit.

title: cpulimit
text: Limit the CPU of a process without touching its priority. cpulimit alternates SIGSTOP and SIGCONT within short chunks and corrects the duty cycle from the CPU time the target actually used, so the limit follows system load. It is made for batch jobs that must not eat the machine. Install Usage Source Version 1.0.3 · GPL-2.0-or-later · release notes # an existing process: half a CPU cpulimit -l 50 -p 1234 # by name, with its children cpulimit -l 25 -i -e ffmpeg # start a command and limit it; the exit status is the command's cpulimit -l 80 -- make -j8 # background daemon with syslog and a pid file cpulimit -d -s -P /run/cpulimit.pid -l 30 -e backup Why this one A fork of Angelo Marletta's cpulimit, kept compatible with it: the options -p -e -l -c -i -m -v -z , the exit statuses and the log lines are unchanged, so existing scripts keep working. Follows the load The next run slice is computed from the CPU time the target really used in the last chunk, not from a fixed duty cycle. How it works Never strands a target Every exit path sends SIGCONT first. The one thing no user-space program can survive is SIGKILL of itself; the FAQ says what to do . Safe identity A process is its pid and start time, so a recycled pid is never limited by mistake, and two limiters cannot fight over one target. Operable Daemon mode with syslog and a pid file, strict option parsing, exit statuses documented in the man page, static musl builds. Tested in the open Unit, integration, fuzz, sanitizer, mutation and model-checking harnesses, with their limits stated. Verification Many systems Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD and Solaris/illumos have an iterator; what is actually tested where is spelled out. Get started git clone https://github.com/denji/cpulimit.git cd cpulimit make && sudo make install cpulimit -l 30 -- gzip -9 big.tar GNU make and a C compiler are all it takes ( gmake on the BSDs and illumos). Install covers static builds, packaging variables and the platform notes; Usage has every option, the exit statuses and worked examples.

title: Install
text: cpulimit builds with GNU make and any C99 compiler. It has no dependencies beyond the C library (and libkvm on FreeBSD). Build and install git clone https://github.com/denji/cpulimit.git cd cpulimit make # binary in build/cpulimit (copied to src/cpulimit) make check # unit, CLI and integration tests sudo make install # /usr/local/bin/cpulimit and the man page On FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD and illumos the GNU make is gmake ( pkg install gmake , pkg_add gmake ); the plain make of those systems cannot read the Makefile. Variables Variable Default Meaning PREFIX /usr/local install prefix; BINDIR and MANDIR derive from it DESTDIR empty staging root for packagers CC , CFLAGS , CPPFLAGS , LDFLAGS -O2 -g yours are never overridden: the flags the program needs ( -D_GNU_SOURCE , -Wall -Wextra ) are kept apart from them BUILD build object and output directory; the build is non-recursive and rebuilds when the compiler or any flag changes WERROR=1 off turn warnings into errors (what CI uses) STATIC_CC musl-gcc compiler for make static make install never calls sudo itself. make uninstall removes what it installed. Static binary make static STATIC_CC=musl-gcc # build/static/cpulimit, no shared libraries make static-install The static build uses its own object directory, so it never mixes with a dynamic one. Release binaries Tagged releases are meant to carry static musl binaries (x86_64, aarch64, armv7, i686, ppc64le, s390x, riscv64) with a .sha256 file each. The release workflow has not produced a release yet, so look at the releases page to see whether one exists for your version before relying on it. How to check a download: Releases . Notes for packagers The man page is hand written ( man/cpulimit.1 ) and installed by make install ; make man only checks that it formats. make check needs /proc (Linux) or the platform's process interface; the integration tests start real processes. SKIP_INTEGRATION=1 runs only the unit tests, and CPULIMIT_SKIP_TIMING=1 skips the checks that depend on CPU accounting being accurate (emulated CPUs, busy shared builders). The version is in three places that a test keeps equal: src/cli/cli.c , the man page header and the top of CHANGELOG.md . Which systems are tested All of Linux (glibc and musl), macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD and NetBSD have a process iterator; the honest version of how much each was run is on the platforms page . Short form: Linux is tested heavily, macOS and OpenBSD run the unit tests in CI, FreeBSD and the other BSDs are built and report their results to a non-gating workflow, and NetBSD and Solaris/illumos have not yet been confirmed on a real system.

title: Platforms
text: A process iterator exists for Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD and Solaris/illumos. How much each has been run differs a lot, and this page says so instead of rounding up. Status Platform Status Evidence Linux, glibc tested CI on x86_64 and arm64; gcc and clang; -O0 , -O2 , -O3 ; -std=gnu99 to gnu2x ; sanitizers, valgrind, fuzzing, stress Linux, musl CI x86_64, i386, arm64, armv7, ppc64le, s390x, riscv64 (qemu-user except x86_64, which fakes parts of /proc ) macOS 14, 15 unit tests CI builds and runs the unit tests, not the integration tests. The job does not gate a release. OpenBSD 7.9, 8.0 unit tests CI builds with -Werror and runs the unit tests and the command-mode tests in a VM. 7.9 passes; on 8.0 one timing bound failed once and was relaxed, so 8.0 is not yet confirmed with the final code. Does not gate a release. FreeBSD 14, 15 builds CI builds on 14.1; the vm workflow (manual and weekly) builds and tests 14.5 and 15.1. The iterator was reworked in 1.0.3 and has not been run on FreeBSD since. NetBSD 10, 11 not yet run Written from the NetBSD sources, sharing code with OpenBSD. Some facts (zombie status value, the clock rate source) are assumptions until the first run. HardenedBSD, GhostBSD report only Built by the vm workflow; they should select the FreeBSD code. Solaris, OmniOS, OpenIndiana never run An iterator was contributed by Jim Mason; it has never been compiled in CI. The vm workflow is the first attempt, and its compiler package names are guesses. DragonFly BSD unsupported No iterator. Its kinfo_proc and clock units are not confirmed. GNU/Hurd, Haiku unsupported Probed only. Haiku's team info has no parent pid, so -i cannot work there as designed. "Does not gate a release" means a failure of that job is reported but does not stop a tag from producing release assets. The current results of every job are on the Actions page ; this page does not copy them. The vm workflow Hosted CI has no BSD or illumos runners, so the repository runs those systems in QEMU virtual machines (the vmactions actions). The workflow vm.yml is experimental and report only: it runs by hand ( Actions → vm → Run workflow ) and weekly. Each job builds, runs the unit tests and copies its transcript back, which is shown as an annotation on the run, so a failure can be read without opening raw logs. It also runs the full suite, integration tests included, on Debian for riscv64, ppc64le and aarch64 under system emulation, where /proc is real, and probes GNU/Hurd and Haiku. Platform notes OpenBSD and NetBSD No libkvm and no special group: the iterator reads sysctl kern.proc (NetBSD: kern.proc2 ). CPU time comes from the statistics tick counters, divided by the statistics clock rate. They are sampled at randomised instants, so one 50 ms sample can show five to seven ticks; the unit test allows for that on OpenBSD (usage bound 1.7 instead of 1.2). Zombies are listed by the kernel and are skipped ( p_stat dead/zombie). Without that, command mode waited on children that had already ended. macOS CPU time is reported in mach absolute time units, which are nanoseconds on Intel but not on Apple silicon; the iterator converts with the timebase. Inspecting another user's process needs privilege; a process that cannot be inspected is skipped. Linux containers The target must be visible in your PID namespace and signalable. Inside a container, -e matches processes of that container only. If the container's cgroup has a CPU quota, that quota applies as well; cpulimit adds to it, it does not replace it. Adding a platform A port is one file, src/platform/<os>/iterator.c , plus a branch in src/platform/iterator.c . It must provide init_process_iterator , get_next_process and close_process_iterator and fill struct process (pid, parent pid, a start time that is only ever compared for equality, CPU time in milliseconds). Take a snapshot if the system allows it and call snapshot_select() for the filter; skip zombies and kernel threads. The checklist is in Contributing .

title: Releases
text: The full history is CHANGELOG.md . The command-line interface and the exit statuses documented in man cpulimit are the public interface that 1.x keeps stable ( semantic versioning ). 1.0.3 2026-10-28 OpenBSD and NetBSD support, one shared selection of a process and its descendants for all iterators, a FreeBSD iterator that follows the whole tree under -i (it stopped at the direct children before), clang-format, a wider CI matrix of virtual machines. Options, exit statuses and log text unchanged. 1.0.2 2026-10-24 Source tree reorganized by role, CI and benchmark workflows repaired, CBMC moved to its own workflow. No change to options, exit statuses or log text. 1.0.1 2026-10-22 The bounded model checker found a real defect: compute_slices() computed 0 / NaN and cleaned it up afterwards. It now never produces a NaN; the result is identical for every input. Verification harnesses reworked. 1.0.0 2026-10-21 First release of the fork: daemon mode, syslog, pid file, single-limiter lock, single-process command mode, strict option parsing, pid and start-time identity, a rewritten /proc reader, a non-recursive build, GitHub Actions instead of Travis. Moving between versions: Upgrading . Verify a download Release assets are static musl binaries named cpulimit-ARCH-linux-musl , each with a .sha256 file. The release workflow has not produced a release yet; if the releases page lists assets, check them like this: sha256sum -c cpulimit-x86_64-linux-musl.sha256 chmod +x cpulimit-x86_64-linux-musl && ./cpulimit-x86_64-linux-musl -V The checksum guards against a damaged download, not against a compromised release page. Building from source remains the reference: make && make check && sudo make install .

title: Upgrading
text: Log lines, exit statuses and the options -p -e -l -c -i -m -v -z are unchanged from the original, so existing scripts keep working. These are the differences a script or an operator can notice. From 1.0.2 to 1.0.3 Nothing to change. Options, exit statuses and log text are the same, and the controller is the same. FreeBSD: -i now limits the whole tree. It used to limit only the direct children of the target, so grandchildren ran free. If you relied on that, limit the child you want by pid instead. New systems: OpenBSD and NetBSD build and run; see Platforms for how far each is tested. From the original cpulimit (0.2.x, 0.3.2) Area Original 1.x Option values atoi : -l 5x and -l abc were accepted, and -m could crash strict parsing with ranges; -c 0 and -c 1000000 or more are rejected instead of spinning or failing in nanosleep Command mode a separate limiter process that could outlive its parent one process; the exit status is the command's Two limiters, one target allowed; they undo each other's SIGSTOP / SIGCONT the second is refused (exit 1) and names the first; --no-lock restores the old behaviour Process identity pid only: a reused pid was limited as if it were the target pid and start time Signals handled in the handler; a signal could be lost before the wait flag-only handler; signals blocked except inside pselect() Clock wall clock CLOCK_MONOTONIC New options none -d , -s , -P , --no-lock , --no-boost , -V , and long options for all Build recursive Makefiles, Travis CI one Makefile, GitHub Actions Control accuracy is the same: both versions use one controller, and both under-deliver at low limits and overshoot near 50 %. The gain is the lower cost of the limiter itself ( measurements ). Checking an upgrade cpulimit -V # version cpulimit -l 50 -- sh -c 'exit 7'; echo $? # 7: the command's status is passed through cpulimit -l 5x -p 1234 ; echo $? # 1: strict option parsing

title: Usage
text: Exactly one target: a pid ( -p ), an executable name or path ( -e ), or a command that cpulimit starts and limits. man cpulimit is the reference; this page adds the reasoning and examples. Synopsis cpulimit [OPTIONS...] -p PID cpulimit [OPTIONS...] -e NAME_OR_PATH cpulimit [OPTIONS...] [--] COMMAND [ARGS...] Options Option Meaning -l, --limit=N Allowed CPU in percent of one CPU, 0 to 100 × the number of CPUs (150 means one and a half CPUs). Required. -p, --pid=N Limit this pid. Implies -z . -e, --exe=FILE Limit the process whose executable has this name (matched against the basename) or this full path. cpulimit never selects itself. -c, --chunk-size=N Control chunk in microseconds, 1 to 1000000, default 100000. Shorter chunks follow the limit more closely and cost more wake-ups. -i, --include-children Also limit the descendants of the target. They are found again on every cycle, so children started later are picked up. -m, --minimum-limited-cpu=M Processes using less than M of one CPU ( 0.05 means 5 %) are left running instead of being stopped. Note the unit differs from -l . Default 0. -z, --lazy Exit when there is no target or it terminates, instead of waiting for one to appear. -d, --daemon Detach and run in the background. Not valid with a command. -s, --syslog Also send events to syslog, facility LOG_DAEMON . -P, --pidfile=FILE Write the daemon's pid (needs -d ). A pid file naming a live process is refused, a stale one is replaced, and it is removed on a normal exit. --no-lock Allow a target that another cpulimit already limits. --no-boost Do not try to raise cpulimit's own scheduling priority. -v, -V, -h Verbose statistics, print the version, print the usage text ( -h exits 1, as every release has). Numbers are parsed strictly: -l 5x , -l abc , an empty value, and values out of range are usage errors (exit 1), not silently read as 5 or 0. Examples An existing process cpulimit -l 50 -p 1234 # half a CPU; exits when pid 1234 ends cpulimit -l 200 -p 1234 # two CPUs' worth, for a multi-threaded target By name cpulimit -l 25 -e ffmpeg # waits for ffmpeg to appear, limits it cpulimit -l 25 -z -e ffmpeg # exits at once if there is none cpulimit -l 25 -i -e make # make and everything it spawns A command cpulimit -l 80 -- make -j8 # exit status is make's cpulimit -l 30 -i -- ./build.sh # the script and its children In command mode there is exactly one cpulimit process; the command is its child. Its exit status comes straight from waitpid() , and if it was killed by a signal the raw wait status is returned, as before. As a service cpulimit -d -s -P /run/cpulimit.pid -l 30 -e backup kill "$(cat /run/cpulimit.pid)" # SIGTERM: releases the target, exits 0 Exit statuses Status Meaning 0 Released the target after SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP or SIGQUIT; -z found no target; -V . 1 Usage error, a target that is already limited, or a target that is cpulimit itself. Also -h . 2 The control loop failed (an allocation or a system call). other In command mode: the command's own status. Signals SIGINT , SIGTERM , SIGHUP and SIGQUIT make cpulimit send SIGCONT to every process it has been limiting, then exit. A signal that was already ignored when cpulimit started (for example SIGHUP under nohup ) stays ignored. SIGPIPE is ignored, so a closed stdout cannot kill the limiter while a target is stopped. One limiter per target Two limiters on the same process undo each other's stop and continue, so the second is refused (exit 1) with the pid of the first. The lock is an fcntl record lock in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/cpulimit/ (or /tmp/cpulimit-<euid>/ ), keyed on pid and start time. It disappears with its holder, even on SIGKILL , so there are no stale locks. --no-lock overrides it. Permissions cpulimit signals the target, so it needs the privilege to do so: the same user, or root. Started on a process of another user without that privilege, -p prints Process found but you aren't allowed to control it , touches nothing, and waits or (with -z , which -p implies) exits. A process that becomes unsignalable while it is being limited is treated like one that has exited: it is dropped from the group, and the only trace is a line with -v ( SIGSTOP failed. Process N dead! ). Unless --no-boost is given, cpulimit also tries to lower its own nice value so its timing is not delayed by the load it is limiting. This needs privilege; when it is refused, cpulimit carries on and says so only with -v ( Cannot change priority. Run as root or renice for best results. ). It never changes the nice value, I/O class, CPU affinity or scheduling policy of the target ; the integration tests check that for nice , ionice , taskset and chrt . Choosing -c and -m The default chunk of 100 ms is a good start. Shorter chunks smooth the load of the target at the price of more wake-ups; very long chunks make a stalled target visible to users and timeouts. -m is for trees with many idle children ( -i ): idle processes are not worth a stop/continue every chunk, and leaving them running costs nothing because they use almost no CPU.

title: Verification
text: Everything here is in the repository and wired into CI. Nothing is claimed as proved beyond what the tools actually reported, and the limits are listed next to the results. Current status The results of every run are on the Actions page; this page does not copy them. Figures below were measured on a Linux x86_64 development host unless they say otherwise. Techniques Technique Covers Unit, CLI and integration tests ( make check ) controller, /proc parser, process table, list, CLI, lock, snapshot selection, 55 end-to-end checks with real processes, and 123 checks of cpulimit together with nice , ionice , taskset , chrt , env , nohup , timeout and setsid Sanitizers ASan and UBSan on gcc and clang; clang's integer sanitizers Fuzzing the stat parser and the CLI parser against stated properties, not only "no crash" (libFuzzer in CI, a standalone driver locally) Bounded model checking CBMC harnesses for the controller invariants, tick conversion and the /proc parser ( cbmc.yml , manual and weekly). experimental The same harnesses run as random tests on every push ( make verif-sim ). Mutation testing defects re-introduced one at a time, each of which must fail a unit test: 25 mutants, all detected locally Coverage gcov line and branch coverage with an 85 % line gate Stress and valgrind fork/exit churn under -i with 300 children: no leaks, flat memory, nothing left stopped Static analysis gcc -fanalyzer (must be silent), clang-tidy, cppcheck, scan-build, CodeQL Format clang-format 18 checked in CI ( make format-check ) Portability CI matrix of OS, compiler, libc and architecture; the experimental vm workflow Measurements Every number is in data/results.json with where and when it was measured, and the charts are drawn from that file by tools/charts.py . They are single runs on a 2-CPU virtual machine with a 10 ms clock tick: treat differences of a point or two as noise. Accuracy. A one-thread busy loop under -l N , 8 s per case. The two versions are the same within noise: both overshoot near 50 % and under-deliver at 10 % and 25 %, because they share one controller. Nothing here is an improvement. Overhead. The gain is in what the limiter itself costs: fewer system calls, and half the CPU with 200 children under -i . The single-target CPU figure is close to the noise floor (an earlier run measured the baseline at 0.12 %), so only the system-call and -i rows were stable across runs. Measured on 1.0.0 against upstream 0.3.2 and not repeated for later releases. Coverage (tools/coverage.sh (gcov), 2026-10-29, make coverage on 1.0.3 including daemon children). runtime/daemon.c and main.c are the weakest; they hold the process and signal plumbing that is hardest to drive from tests. Bugs found by the process The bounded model checker found compute_slices() computing 0 / NaN and cleaning it up afterwards (fixed in 1.0.1, the result is identical for every input). Property checks found ticks_to_ms() returning a negative number for ticks = 2^63 + 1 at 1000 Hz and saturating wrongly above 1.8e16 ticks per second (neither reachable with a real clock rate). The OpenBSD runs exposed that p_rtime only advances in scheduling-quantum steps and that zombies are listed; both are fixed and explained under platform notes . Not verified Nothing is "proved". One CBMC harness has finished (the field positions of a well-formed stat line, within its bounds, CI run 39890593464); the others were narrowed and have no verdict yet. The harnesses cover three pure functions, not the control loop or signal handling. macOS, FreeBSD, NetBSD and Solaris/illumos code has not been run by hand; see the platform table for what CI ran. musl on non-x86 runs under qemu-user, which fakes parts of /proc ; some process-name tests are skipped there. Real syslog delivery is not tested. No ACSL/Frama-C specification exists, and AFL++ was not run. The benchmark was measured once on a shared VM, on 1.0.0.
